Let’s talk about something that sneaks up on a lot of us—especially if you’re someone who loves to help, or works in a caregiving role.
Chapter 7: Dealing with “Benevolent” Traps—the problem of good intentions.
Here’s the thing. When your heart’s in the right place, it’s easy to fall into what I like to call a “benevolent trap.” You know, those situations where your drive to help, be reliable, or always go the extra mile turns into a source of ongoing stress? It starts out feeling good—maybe you volunteer for extra work, or you’re the friend who’s always there with a listening ear. People praise your dedication, and that feels rewarding.
But, over time, have you noticed how the more you give, the more everyone seems to expect? And suddenly, stepping back feels almost impossible. You might even start to feel resentful, or just plain worn out.
Take the example of a nurse who’s always saying yes to extra shifts. At first, she’s seen as a hero. But after a while, she’s exhausted, maybe even frustrated, and her own needs get pushed aside. Or think about that friend who’s always available—she’s supportive, but her own struggles? They rarely get airtime.
So, how do you escape these traps without losing your caring nature?
First, start by recognizing the pattern. If helping others is leaving you drained or resentful, it’s time to pause and check in with yourself.
Next, try setting compassionate boundaries. Remember, it’s absolutely possible to support people you care about without sacrificing your own well-being.
Don’t be afraid to communicate your needs clearly. Let others know when you need a break, or when you could use a little support yourself.
And maybe the toughest part— allow others to step up. Trust that it’s okay to step back sometimes; the world won’t fall apart if you take a breather.
Here’s a metaphor that really brings it home: Think about the oxygen mask instructions on an airplane. You’re always told to put your own mask on first, before helping anyone else. Why? Because you can’t help others if you’re running out of air yourself.
Taking care of your own needs first isn’t selfish—it’s the smart, sustainable way to keep showing up for the people and causes you care about.
So, next time you feel yourself slipping into one of those benevolent traps, just remember the oxygen mask. Secure yours first. That way, you’ll have the energy to keep helping others—without losing yourself along the way.
